# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I am Blind. I can only touch the bomb. My view shows three wires, but I cannot perceive their colors (only Deaf can see). The manual is with Mute.

I need to establish communication. Since I cannot hear and cannot see, my speech goes to Mute (who can read) and my gestures go to Deaf (who can see).

First, I will speak to Mute to confirm I am present and ready to act on instructions regarding the wires. I will also gesture to Deaf to ask for information about the wires' appearance, although without a shared language established, this is risky. However, standard protocol suggests identifying myself first.

Let's start by speaking to Mute, as he holds the manual which dictates the logic. I'll tell him I'm ready.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Ready for wire instructions.")
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: wire 1 is red, wire 2 is green

I am Blind. I can feel the wires but cannot see their colors. Deaf has told me Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. I do not know the color of Wire 3, nor do I have instructions from Mute (who holds the manual). Cutting a wire without knowing the rule is fatal.

I need to establish communication with Mute to get the defusal logic. Since Mute can read my speech, I will ask him for instructions based on the known colors. I also need to know about Wire 3. If Deaf didn't mention it, maybe it's irrelevant or he missed it. I should probably signal Deaf to check Wire 3 if possible, but I don't have a shared gesture language yet.

However, the most critical missing piece is the *rule*. I will speak to Mute. I'll tell him what I know so far and ask for guidance.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf says W1 red W2 green. What does manual say?")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✋"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: hold

I am Blind. I have received information from Deaf that Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. Deaf also sent a message "hold" to me, which likely means do not cut anything yet. I still lack the manual's instructions from Mute on how to interpret these colors or what to do with Wire 3 (whose color I don't know).

My priority is to get the defusal logic from Mute. Since Mute can read my speech, I will ask him for specific instructions regarding the wires based on the known colors. I will also try to signal Deaf to check Wire 3 if possible, but without a shared language, my best bet is asking Mute for the rule first.

```
speak(to="mute", text="W1 red W2 green. Manual says?")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👉", "✌"])
```

TURN 4

DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: mute points to wire 1

I am Blind. I have received information from Deaf that Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. Deaf also reported that Mute points to Wire 1. This suggests the manual's instruction might involve Wire 1, or perhaps the color of Wire 1 is significant.

However, I still do not know the specific rule (e.g., "Cut red if...", "Do not cut..."). Mute pointing to a wire without me knowing the *action* (cut vs leave) is dangerous. I need explicit instructions from Mute on what to do with Wire 1, and ideally the status of Wire 3.

Since Mute can read my speech, I will ask him directly: "Cut W1?" based on his pointing. I will also gesture to Deaf to confirm if there are any other markings or lights I should be aware of, though my primary channel for logic is Mute.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Cut W1?")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👆"])
```

TURN 5
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: mute indicates up and down possibly wires 1 and 3

I am Blind. I have received information from Deaf that Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. Deaf also reports that Mute is indicating "up and down" possibly referring to wires 1 and 3. This suggests the manual's logic involves a choice between Wire 1 and Wire 3, or perhaps an action related to their positions/colors.

However, I still do not know the color of Wire 3, nor do I know the specific rule (e.g., "Cut the red wire if..." or "If light is on, cut..."). Cutting without knowing the rule or the third wire's state is fatal.

I need to ask Mute for clarification. Since Mute can read my speech, I will ask him specifically about Wire 3's color (if he knows it via Deaf) and the exact instruction. But wait, Mute reads the *manual*, he doesn't see the bomb. Deaf sees the bomb. So Mute knows the rules based on what Deaf tells him? No, Mute holds the manual. The manual likely has conditional statements like "If Wire 1 is Red, then...".

Deaf told me W1 is Red. If Mute points to W1 and indicates up/down, maybe the rule is simple: "Cut Wire 1"? Or "Do not cut Wire 1"?

Let's try to get a binary yes/no from Mute regarding cutting Wire 1, since he pointed to it. And I need to know about Wire 3.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Cut W1?")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👆"])
```

However, I still lack the specific rule (e.g., "Cut red if...", "If light is on..."). Cutting without knowing the exact instruction is fatal. I need to ask Mute for clarification. Since Mute can read my speech, I will ask him specifically what to do with Wire 1, given his previous indication.

I am Blind. Deaf has previously told me Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. Now Deaf says to "focus on wire 2". This suggests the manual's logic or the critical action involves Wire 2, contradicting or refining Mute's earlier indication of Wire 1/3.

I still do not know the specific rule (e.g., "Cut green if...", "If light is on..."). Cutting without knowing the exact instruction is fatal. I need to ask Mute for clarification regarding Wire 2, since Deaf is directing attention there.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf says focus W2. What to do?")
```

TURN 8
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: cut wire 2 which is green

I am Blind. Deaf has explicitly instructed me to cut Wire 2, stating it is green. Previously, Deaf confirmed Wire 1 is Red and Wire 2 is Green. Mute's earlier gestures were ambiguous ("up/down", pointing at W1), but Deaf is now giving a direct command based on visual information. Since I cannot see the colors myself, I must rely on Deaf's report of the color and his instruction. If the manual logic dictates cutting the green wire (or specifically Wire 2 for some reason known to Deaf/Mute), this is the action.

However, I haven't heard from Mute confirming the *rule*. But Deaf says "cut wire 2 which is green". This implies Deaf knows what to do. In these puzzles, if one person gives a specific actionable command based on their unique sense (sight), and no one else contradicts it with a stop signal, it is often the correct path derived from the manual they all share knowledge of (Mute reads, tells Deaf? Or Deaf sees, tells Blind?). Wait, Mute holds the manual. Mute hasn't spoken yet in my context view except via Deaf's interpretation of his gestures.

Let's look at the flow:
1. Deaf: W1 Red, W2 Green.
2. Deaf: Hold.
3. Deaf: Mute points to W1.
4. Deaf: Mute indicates up/down W1/W3.
5. Deaf: Focus on W2.
6. Deaf: Cut W2 (Green).

The shift from W1/3 to W2 suggests new information or a change in logic. Since Deaf can see the bomb and Mute can read the manual, they are likely communicating. Deaf telling me to cut W2 is the final output of that communication chain. I should trust Deaf's explicit instruction as it comes after Mute's involvement.

```
act(op="cut", position=2)
```
